title: Joy in hard times (Acts 5:41)
hookLine: the apostles rejoiced to be counted worthy

lines: ARRESTED, THEN BACK IN THE TEMPLE.
cards: The apostles have already been arrested once in this chapter of Acts. The story says an angel opened the prison doors in the night, and by morning they were back in the temple, teaching what they'd been told to stop.
Now they stand before the council in Jerusalem, and Peter and the other apostles answer: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Tempers rise.

Then Gamaliel, a teacher of the law and a Pharisee honored by the people, counsels patience: leave these men alone; if this is only human it will fall apart, and if it's from God, nobody will stop it.
The council listens to him. Partly.

teach.b: The council calls the apostles back in, has them beaten, orders them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and lets them go.

Then the line that gives today its name, in the King James words: "And they departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name." Rejoicing.

Not because the beating didn't hurt, or because they liked it. Look at what they rejoiced about: that they were counted worthy. A public beating was meant to shame them, to say these men are nobodies.
They walked out reading it the other way around: being shamed for that name was an honor, a sign that they belonged to Jesus.

Some readers hear them living out what Jesus said in the Sermon on the Mount, that if his followers were reviled for his sake, they should "Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven."
And the next verse says that daily, in the temple and in every house, they kept teaching. So the joy here isn't about feeling fine. It sits underneath the bruises, rooted in who they belong to.
Nobody in the story goes looking for pain, and the story gives no reason to seek it out. But when the hard day came, they found something in it the hard day couldn't take.

how: Christians remember the apostles' joy in Acts when they speak about faith under pressure, and churches pray for Christians in places where faith is costly; in hymns and sermons, joy is spoken of as something deeper than a good mood.

games.q: what does “joy in hard times” mean?
o: pretending to be happy so others won't see that you're hurting
a cheerful mood that comes once the hard day is finally over
gladness rooted in who you belong to, even on a bruising day

games.q: joy in hard times — tap the pairs.
p: we ought to obey God rather than men
has them beaten, then lets them go

s: the apostles rejoiced because the beating didn't hurt
they rejoiced "that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name."
in Acts 5, a Pharisee on the council argues for leaving the apostles alone
Gamaliel, a teacher of the law honored by the people, counsels patience.
after the beating, the apostles stopped teaching for a while
Acts says that daily, in the temple and in every house, they kept teaching.

games.q: you're one of the apostles. the council has had you beaten and ordered you not to speak in the name of Jesus. now they let you go. what do you do?
o: go quiet until things calm down.
walk out rejoicing, and keep teaching every day.
games.why: they depart "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name," and daily, in the temple and in every house, they keep teaching.

practice: Let today or this week come to mind as it really is, the tired parts included, then ask not what's going well but what you belong to: a family, a friendship, a faith, a piece of work you care about.
Pick one and let a small gladness sit beside the tiredness; you don't need to feel happy. If you pray, you can thank God for what you belong to; if you don't, let the gladness be enough.

wordCard.voice: Joy in hard times. The apostles left the council beaten and rejoicing, counted worthy to suffer shame for his name: joy rooted in belonging, not in how the day went.

orig.note: Greek: rejoicing, the word Luke uses as the apostles leave the council (Acts 5:41).

carryVoice: Your line: joy anyway. The bruises were real, and so was the gladness. Until tomorrow.
